text:
Luis Enrique is in uncharted territory, even if he insists that “it isn’t a first”. Since arriving at Paris Saint-Germain in 2023, only three players have spent more than 100 days on the sideline – Nuno Mendes, Lucas Hernandez and Presnel Kimpembe – and only Mendes is an important first-team player. But for the remainder of the season, or at least the vast majority of it, Luis Enrique must do without two of his stars: Désiré Doué and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.
Doué arrived in Nice on Saturday evening already bearing scars. The PSG forward wore a mouth guard after Davide Frattesi had dislodged one of his front teeth with a stray arm during France’s defeat by Italy during the international break.
He showed it off to the crowd when he tapped home an Achraf Hakimi cross to give PSG a 2-1 lead a mere 24 seconds after Senny Mayulu had levelled the score from the spot for PSG. Just six minutes later, without making any contact with the oncoming Sofiane Diop, Doué was left screaming on the floor, clutching his right knee.
The Nice players Alidu Seidu and Youssouf Ndayishimiye, both of whom have sustained ACL injuries in recent times, quickly grasped the severity of the injury, the nature of which was confirmed on Sunday. Tests revealed an ACL tear that will probably rule Doué out until the end of the season; Kvaratskhelia suffered the same fate last month.
“We have other players in our squad. We will overcome it as a team,” said Luis Enrique, who added that they are “open” to dipping into the market. Eli Junior Kroupi is being linked with a move from Bournemouth to the Parc des Princes, but should the two-time European champions opt against recruiting this winter, it will be a test of the club’s continued assertion that “the star is the collective”. That mantra belies a continued level of spending at PSG that far outstrips their domestic competitors and an accumulation of talent that led Nice’s manager, Olivier Pantaloni, to describe them as a “club apart” in Ligue 1.
Pantaloni noted PSG’s capacity to turn on “at the press of a button”, which left him in no doubt that PSG would “steamroll” the domestic competition once again this year. His side’s 3-2 defeat at their hands, although valiant, reasserts a hierarchy that no one questions, injuries or no injuries.
Ligue 1 may not challenge PSG but, shorn of two of their most technically gifted players, top European sides will. Even in domestic games, wins have oftentimes relied on call-in-the-cavalry hour, with Ousmane Dembélé, Kvaratskhelia, Vitinha and the like unleashed against already exhausted defences to seal the win. Their victories over Le Mans and Strasbourg, notably, were obtained in this manner.
The serious injuries sustained by Doué and Kvaratskhelia mean there is no longer a cavalry to call upon. PSG will also have to change their contentious policy of resting key players in domestic competition. Will Dembélé have to play more, and can his body sustain it? That is one question among many.
Mika Godts has said he has time on his side to establish himself at PSG. Not any more. Will he step up? Will Ferran Torres, who scored PSG’s third in their 3-2 win against Nice, rediscover his early-season form? Is Mayulu, fresh from making his France debut, ready? Is Nuno Mendes a viable option on the left wing? And can Maghnes Akliouche, who has so quickly curried favour with Luis Enrique, add goals and assists to his impressive performances?
The answers to these questions will determine PSG’s ability to challenge for a third consecutive Champions League title. Diminished in quantity and quality, PSG’s forward line no longer looks the best in Europe.
It was the abject failure of the Neymar-Kylian Mbappé-Lionel Messi frontline that forged the concept of the modern-day PSG. Star quality was not a guarantor of success; the system, it was decided, would be king. In the absence of Doué and Kvaratskhelia, the limits of this accepted truth will be tested this season.
 
Talking points
Several French clubs used the international break to correct their course. Lens called time on the failed Yannick Cahuzac experiment and brought in Didier Digard, fresh from his sacking at bottom side Le Havre. Strasbourg pulled the plug on Hugo Oliveira after 10 games and hired Vítor Matos from Swansea City to become their fourth manager of 2026. Valérien Ismaël has replaced Digard at Le Havre. And Lyon, whose hand was forced by Paulo Fonseca’s wish to manage boyhood club Sporting, welcomed Carlos Vicens, formerly part of Pep Guardiola’s backroom staff.
Vicens was the only manager to secure all three points on his debut, winning 1-0 at Davide Ancelotti’s Lille. In doing so, the Spaniard became the first manager in Lyon’s history to arrive mid-season and beat a top-flight side in his first away match. Lens showed promise in their 1-1 draw against Toulouse but were denied three points by an inspired performance from goalkeeper Guillaume Restes. There are no signs of revival at Le Havre, who lost 3-1 to promoted side Troyes – or at Strasbourg, who were beaten 1-0 by Brest at the Meinau. Chelsea’s partner club currently occupy the relegation playoff spot.
Five consecutive wins in Ligue 1 had lifted spirits in Marseille, but Bruno Génésio had warned that the revival teetered on a “knife’s edge”. An excellent Le Mans exposed their fragility. Goals from Amine Gouiri and Igor Paixão gave Marseille a 2-0 lead only for Le Mans to run riot in the final quarter of the game and win 3-2.
Patrick Videira’s side secured all three points thanks to Jean Vercruysse’s dramatic 95th-minute winner. “There is a global phenomenon of fragility as soon as we concede a goal,” was Génésio’s explanation for Marseille’s collapse. For Videira, Marseille represent the biggest scalp of his managerial career, although draws against Nice, Lens, and Monaco had already shown the club’s ability to compete at this level.
